title: The country house in Cheadle that inspired Agatha Christie's work

input.summary: Known as the Queen of Crime, her murder mysteries have captivated audiences for more than a century
input.evidence_text: The country house in Cheadle that inspired Agatha Christie's work - BBC News Image caption, Agatha Christie wrote 78 crime novels that have sold an estimated 2 billion copies in 44 languages By Jen Dale BBC Radio Manchester Published 47 minutes ago Known as the Queen of Crime, Agatha Christie murder mysteries have captivated audiences for more than a century. But it might come as a surprise to some that many of her stories were inspired by a country house in Cheadle, Greater Manchester. Abney Hall is the subject of a new episode of Hidden Manchester on BBC Sounds after the Cheadle Civic Society erected an information board in the grounds explaining the novelist's connections. In 1902, Christie first arrived at Abney Hall when she was about 11 years old as her older sister Madge lived at the house after marrying into the wealthy Watts family. Nestled in the village of Cheadle, the gothic building has high-ceilinged rooms, gold chandeliers and a red velvet carpet running down the centre of a large wooden staircase. Outside, there are crosses etched into the stone walls as well as distinctive chimney stacks - no doubt the inspiration for one of her stories The Secret of Chimneys. Image source, Cheadle Civic Society Image caption, Abney Hall and the surrounding gardens forms part of a new heritage trail Trever Evers, from the society, said there were plenty of features to inspire the writer. "You know Abney Hall had it all, it had a waterfall, it had a tunnel under the drive," he said. "She loved the fact that the house had back passageways and staircases that they used to hide from each other." Evers added that the geography of Abney Hall was itself an inspiration. "All the time we were there we had the media, we had Swampy, we were able to give our message that this is a terrible idea, 400 acres of green belt disappearing," Porter said. title: Man denies charge over Manchester synagogue attack

input.lead: Hekmat Omar Ali Hakim, 49, denied failing to disclose information regarding terrorist activity
input.summary: Hekmat Omar Ali Hakim, 49, denied failing to disclose information regarding terrorist activity
input.evidence_text: Man denies charge over Manchester synagogue attack - BBC News Image source, PA Media Image caption, The charges are linked to the 2 October 2025 attack By Paul Burnell North West Published 21 August 2026 A man has denied failing to disclose information in relation to the Manchester synagogue attack. Hekmat Omar Ali Hakim appeared before Westminster Magistrates' Court and pleaded not guilty to failing to disclose information regarding terrorist activity. The 49-year-old, of St James Road in Higher Broughton, Salford, spoke only to confirm his name and indicate his plea. He was remanded into custody to appear at at the Old Bailey on 25 September. Worshippers Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby were killed when Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, a Syrian-born British citizen, drove into the gates of the Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation Synagogue on 2 October. He then began attacking with a knife, while wearing a fake suicide belt, before being shot dead by police outside the synagogue. First direct charge Sally-Anne Russell, prosecuting, alleged CCTV evidence of conversations between Hakim and Al-Shamie show him "condoning and supporting" the terrorist action. Hakim attended the same mosque as Al-Shamie and travelled in a car with him on various occasions before the attack, which took place on Yom Kippur, one of the holiest day of the Jewish religious calender Cravitz, 66, died from knife wounds inflicted by Al-Shamie while Daulby, 53, was struck by a single gunshot wound to the chest fired by an armed police officer scrambled to the scene in the Crumpsall area of the city. Three other men were treated in hospital for serious injuries. Greater Manchester Police said there have so far been eight arrests in connection with the attack, however this is the first charge that "relates directly".

V News Neal Keeling Chief reporter 07:16, 22 Aug 2026 In his darkest of times Tony Wilson was still capable of a good quote. He was fighting for his life after developing renal cancer when he delivered a memorable quip Doctors had suggested he take Sutent. It would not provide a cure but would extend his life. But Manchester Primary Care Trust refused to fund the £3,500 per month cost of the drug. Yet patients alongside him at The Christie Hospital and living in Cheshire did receive funding Music industry and media friends rallied to help pay. Branding the situation a scandal Wilson pointed out that tummy tucks were available on the NHS, and said at the time: " I thought where am I going to find the money? I'm the one person in this industry who famously has never m He never paid for private health care because he was a socialist. Wilson died on August 10th 2007 aged 57 after the cancer progressed and he suffered a heart attack On his Peter Saville designed headstone in Manchester's Southern Cemetery it says: "Broadcaster Cultural Catalyst". His part in Manchester's renaissance from post-industrial gloom was huge

input.evidence_text: Every new trader in the city reaches the same fork eventually. Two boxes on a registrar’s page, one ending .co.uk, one ending .com, both available, both costing roughly the price of a round. The choice looks cosmetic, and it gets treated that way It is the one decision in building a business website that follows you everywhere afterwards: invoices, email signatures, van livery, the card in the window. Changing it later means redirects, reprinted stationery and a few uneasy months while search engines work out which addres Most owners settle it on availability, and if the name is taken on .com and free on .co.uk, that is usually that. Registrars bundle the domain with hosting and a small business website builder , so the extension gets picked in the same five minutes as the template and the colour Google is unusually direct about this. Its own documentation lists country-code domains as a strong signal that a site is intended for a particular country, notes that server location then stops mattering, and puts the catch in the same table: a country domain can only target one For a Manchester small business selling to people who can drive to the door, that ceiling is the point of the thing rather than a restriction on it. A .co.uk address tells a search engine, and a customer scanning results on a phone at a bus stop, that this is a British operation The constraint bites later, if at all. A trader who picks up wholesale customers in Rotterdam, or starts posting orders to Dublin, finds the same signal now working against the traffic they want, and no setting anywhere undoes it

title: Bolton introduces minimum quality standards for HMOs - Bolton Council

input.lead: Bolton Council is launching a new licensing scheme for landlords of houses in multiple occupation (HMOs)
input.summary: Bolton Council is launching a new licensing scheme for landlords of houses in multiple occupation (HMOs)
input.evidence_text: Bolton Council is launching a new licensing scheme for landlords of houses in multiple occupation (HMOs) The scheme is designed to improve property conditions, strengthen management standards, and ensure tenants have access to safe, high-quality accommodation and was agreed at a meeting of Bolton Council’s Cabinet on Monday (August 17) HMOs are properties that are occupied by three or more people from different households, who share at least one basic amenity i.e. a kitchen, bathroom or toilet - the definition includes bedsits, shared houses and some self–contained flats that did not meet the required standard It is unacceptable that landlords cut corners in critical areas such as failing to obtain fire, gas, and electrical safety certificates or ensuring properties are safe Many landlords operate responsibly, but a substantial proportion of HMOs are poorly managed, unsafe and impact on the community In the past three years, the council has received 1,885 complaints about disrepair in rented homes, typically relating to fire safety, electrical and structural defects, overcrowding, cold and damp, and poor waste management and pest control
